To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) cooperation can collapse when resource variability increases; (ii) cooperation can collapse even when resource abundance is increased; (iii) the combined effect of changes in resource amount and variability can lead to a reinforcement of the initial effect of resource variability on cooperation; (iv) cooperation can be destabilized when resource abundance increases; and (v) cooperation can be reinforced when resource abundance increases, but the initial level of variability in the resource is low.

(1) cooperation is more robust to changes in variability than in abundance, (2) cooperation is more stable in the presence of variability than abundance, (3) a small increase in variability can destabilize cooperation, (4) a small decrease in abundance can destabilize cooperation and (5) the combined effects of abundance and variability can reinforce each other, but also counteract each other, depending on the initial level of social capital and the size of the changes.

Cooperation in a community that harvest resource from a shared pool may be destabilized by an increase in resource abundance, while it may be stabilized by a small increase in variability or scarcity of the resource.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the robustness of self-organized cooperation to global change.
the robustness of norm-driven resource use under environmental variability.
the robustness of norm-driven self-organized cooperation to environmental variability and spatial coupling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cooperation can be robust to variability in resource availability, but that the robustness of a given community depends strongly on the specific biophysical and social conditions.
the effects of global change on cooperation are highly context-dependent, which makes it difficult to make general predictions about its effects on the sustainability of common-pool resource use.
cooperation in the commons is robust to variability, but only if variability does not change too much and is not too large.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cooperation is robust to changes in resource abundance and variability, but not to their combined effects.
the robustness of social norms depends on the interplay between social and biophysical factors, which can lead to counterintuitive outcomes.

cooperation in the commons is robust to changes in the resource abundance and variability, and that it can be stabilized by scarcity and variability, but destabilized by large resource abundance and variability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
norm-driven cooperation in common-pool resource management can be robust against environmental variability and that the effects of environmental change can be complex.
the robustness of norm-driven resource governance is not a simple function of the amount of resource variability, but depends on its magnitude relative to the resource's mean level.
cooperation can be robust against global change and spatial leakage, but only if the community members are able to adapt their behavior to the changing conditions.
